newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr struggles but can't shake rate gloom.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr struggles but can't shake rate gloom.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished Friday on a steady but subdued note as all attempts to get a recovery going were frustrated by offshore offers.

A week after slumping in reaction to depressingly weak retail trade data the currency was still haunted by fears of another domestic rate cut. The first easing on May 23 had been enough for many overseas investors, particularly U.S. investment banks, which had been dumping the dollar ever since.
Corporate and Swiss bank bids had kept US$0.7560 support surprisingly solid in the face of this pressure but dealers felt the odds favoured the downside while a cut remained a risk.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local currency had deflated to US$0.7591/96 having ventured as high as US$0.7617 this morning from US$0.7575/80 late here Thursday.
On the crosses it lost an early bounce to end little changed at 87.80/90 yen having slipped from 8.40/50 on Thursday.

The yen got a late lift from a Nikkei newspaper report that Japan's rising trade surplus would be an issue at the Denver summit on June 20-22 so Japanese authorities might be inclined to encourage yen strength as a way of forestalling criticism.
In trade weighted terms it was a shade firmer at 57.9 from 57.7 late Thursday.

Dealers doubted the dollar could sustain a meaningful rally past US$0.7680 resistance as the prospect of a domestic rate cut and/or a U.S. policy tightening hung like a millstone around the market's neck.

Comments from Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane overnight did nothing to lighten the burden. He said the bank was looking for a pickup in growth in 1997/98 but emphasised the economy had considerable spare capacity, unlike that of the U.S.
Analysts noted such spare capacity implied the economy could grow faster without endangering low inflation, which in turn suggested there was scope for an easier policy if needed.

Macfarlane was also sanguine about the dollar's prospects saying it would follow an essentially flat trend as long as Australia maintained, and it would, an internationally respectable inflation outlook.
Given the bank's confidence on keeping just such an inflation rate, analysts reasoned, it could not be that worried the dollar collapsing if it were to cut rates again.

Whether an easing was needed may be clearer after May jobs data were released next Thursday. The RBA has increasingly emphasised its mandate for curbing unemployment which has remained stubbornly high despite five years of economic growth.
A weak figure, therefore, was sure to stoke speculation of a cut even if employment is a lagging indicator.
In contrast, private banking data suggested April housing finance figures on Wednesday would show a strong rise of around 12 percent, and that was before the last rate cut.

A recovery in the housing market has been a given for some time so even a rise like this would not rule out a cut, but it should feed though into household sales and make an eaisng a little less likely.
The dollar was also under threat from the U.S. where the Federal Reserve is in tightening mode, albeit a gradual one.
Key U.S. payrolls data tonight could decide if the bank hikes at its July 2-3 FOMC meeting.
The stronger the result, and that includes the working week and hourly pay as well as unemployment, the greater the risk of a hike and the more pressure the A$ was likely to come under.

Median forecasts are for payrolls to rise 221,000 after a moderate 142,000 gain in April and for unemployment to edge up to 5.0 percent from 4.9 percent. Analysis of the data will be complicated by significant changes to seasonal factors which might depress May but boost April.
